Screen position, vertical. **The engine owns these while a step is in progress** — it shifts every slot two pixels a frame against the player's motion so they appear to stay put on the map. Writing them mid-step makes an object ride the camera and then snap.

The 40-entry object buffer the game rebuilds every frame and copies to the hardware — four bytes each: y, x, tile id, attributes. **Never write it directly**; the sprite structures above are where a change belongs. Its end is `wTileMap`, and the two being adjacent is a fault the cartridge can fall through.

One past the object buffer — **and it is `wTileMap`'s first byte**. `PrepareOAMData` bounds its clear loop only by comparing the low byte of its write pointer against this address, and nothing bounds the pointer at 40 entries, so a map fielding more than forty sprites walks straight past here and stamps `$A0` into the screen buffer every fourth byte for 256 bytes. A stamped tile is not walkable in any direction.

**The screen, and it reads back as text.** 20x18 tile ids. Gen 1 loads its font so that a tile id *is* the character code of the glyph it draws, and `PlaceString` writes character codes straight in here — so decoding this buffer with the Gen 1 charmap prints exactly what a player can see. That single property is what lets a headless test navigate menus. **Verified live**: the harness decodes it mid-play and counts letters and spaces.

The third of the three blocks a trade exchanges: the offsets inside the party block where a byte had to be substituted, because the preamble byte `$FD` cannot appear in the data. The list is split at offset 252, which is `$FD - 1`, into one part for the Pokemon region and one for the rest.
A copy of the shadow OAM taken before something borrows the sprite hardware, so the overworld can be restored.

One past the live block map. The 1,300 bytes in front of it, with the three-block border the loader leaves on every side, are the rule a map has to obey: `(width + 6) x (height + 6)` blocks must fit. The game's own largest map is 10x72 blocks, which comes to 1,248.

The **top** of the stack. The Stack section is `$DF00-$DFFF` and this label sits at its last byte because the stack pointer starts here and grows downwards through all 256 bytes — which is why the atlas records the 255 bytes below it as reached by no label rather than as a hole.

The OAM DMA routine, copied into high RAM at boot. It has to run from here: the CPU cannot read the cartridge or work RAM while a DMA is in progress, so the loop that waits for it must live somewhere that stays readable.
Counts down while A+B+Start+Select are held; reaching zero resets the game.

One of several unrelated scratch uses sharing this HRAM byte across different routines — elsewhere it also holds `hPreviousTileset` and `hSpriteInterlaceCounter` (see those entries) at different moments; which is live depends on what is currently executing.

Alternates which half of the sprite list is drawn, so more than ten objects on a line flicker instead of vanishing.

Set by `DelayFrame` and cleared by the VBlank handler; the game spins here until it clears. **A machine parked in that loop is usually healthy** — a Game Boy spends most of every frame in it — so finding the CPU here proves nothing on its own.
